Hi Alex - great, thanks for the quick answers and for populating the sheet. Below is a short, actionable explanation that we typically share with customers to avoid metric confusion and to map to unit economics.

Short primer - tokens vs characters vs requests (practical):
- Characters: raw characters are what your telemetry reports today; they're easy to measure but not how inference is billed.
- Tokens: model tokenizer chunks text; tokens roughly correspond to ~4 characters in English on average but varies by language/encoding and punctuation. Billing and model compute are token-based.
- Requests: API calls or end-user interactions; a single request can produce many tokens (prompt + generation) and/or multiple downstream model calls (retrieval + rerank + generation).

Important for billing and $/1M tokens calculations:
- Redwood bills on billed_tokens (prompt_tokens + response_tokens) per API call. If a single user interaction triggers N model calls, we bill the sum of billed_tokens across those calls.
- Prompt caching (what you called "cached prefixes"): if the runtime can serve a cached KV prefix and avoid recomputing those tokens at inference time, you often still transmit the prompt on the wire, but billed_tokens can be reduced depending on cache hit behavior and model/kernel-level caching. Practically:
   - Cold request (no cache): full prompt_tokens + response_tokens billed.
   - Warm/cached prefix: only the incremental tokens that require computation may be billed (depends on how much of the prefix is recovered from KV cache).
   - Note: we don't bill on characters; we convert your avg characters -> tokens using tokenizer estimates in the worksheet.

How we'll handle your numbers and target $/1M tokens:
- Step 1: we'll convert your avg prompt/response chars -> tokens using language-specific factors (we default to 4 chars per token for English as a conservative estimate unless you provide tokenized samples).
- Step 2: we'll multiply tokens per request by requests/month and add multiplier for multi-call fan-out (you mentioned 1.3x).
- Step 3: we'll factor in cache hit rate (45% cached prefixes) and apply conservative billed_token reduction for those hits.
- Step 4: we'll produce cost rows for Hosted API (pay-as-you-go), Dedicated Reserved (committed $/month), and Private (license + infra ops). Each row will show $/month and normalized $/1M billed tokens so you can compare to your target $200- $400 per 1M tokens.

Quick example (illustrative numbers):
- Avg tokens per interaction (after char->token conv): prompt 150 tokens, response 300 tokens => 450 tokens total.
- With 1.3x fan-out -> 585 tokens per end-user interaction.
- With 45% cache hit that reduces billed_tokens by ~30% on those hits -> blended billed_tokens ~ 470 tokens/interaction.
- At 5M interactions/month -> ~2.35B billed_tokens/month.
- If Hosted price = $5 per 1M tokens -> cost ~ $11,750/month; at $100 per 1M tokens (higher-tier model) cost would be much higher.

I'll run your numbers from the sheet and send back a clear $/1M tokens sensitivity table so you can see what model choices and caching buy you.

Attachments: I've updated the pricing CSV with a token conversion column and a cache-adjusted billed_tokens column (redwood_pricing_calc.csv).

Next steps: once you confirm you want the hosted vs dedicated comparison, I'll loop in Rishi to run the Dedicated throughput estimate and show commit pricing that often brings $/1M much lower for sustained volumes.
